title: Learn by Doing: Recursion
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then the past question that traces a recursive method, with its model answer, and the method taught from nothing.
intro:
Part A is the objective questions on this topic. Part B is past questions only: 24/25 asks what compute(13) returns and to show the steps, which is a trace, not a definition.

A recursion question is answered with a two column table: the call, and what it is waiting for.

lockin.big: "Every recursive method needs a base case that returns without calling itself, and a recursive case that moves towards it."
lockin.sub: Trace it as a table of calls going down and answers coming back up. No base case, or one you never reach, is a StackOverflowError.

methodFrames.teach:
A recursive method calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. Two parts, always: the base case, which returns without calling itself, and the recursive case, which moves towards the base case.

public class Recurse {    static int factorial(int n) {        if (n <= 1) return 1;        return n * factorial(n - 1);    }    static int digitSum(int n) {        if (n < 10) return n;        return n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10);    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println(factorial(5));        System.out.println(digitSum(13));    }}
Output120
4
methodFrames.ask: Find both parts in this, then predict the two printed values.

methodFrames.teach: 120 and 4. In factorial the base case is n <= 1; in digitSum it is n < 10, one digit left. Both recursive cases shrink the argument, which is what guarantees the base case is reached.
methodFrames.ask: What happens if the base case is missing, or never reached?

methodFrames.check: It recurses forever and throws StackOverflowError.
methodFrames.teach: The calls pile up until the call stack is full and the program dies with a StackOverflowError. Naming that error is a mark, and "no base case" is a planted error in a debug question.
methodFrames.ask: Now the trace, which is how the paper asks it. Write out digitSum(13) as calls going down and answers coming back.

methodFrames.teach:
Two columns, and both directions matter:

Going downComing back
digitSum(13) needs 3 + digitSum(1)3 + 1 = 4
digitSum(1), and 1 is under 10returns 1

Write the table, then the answer. The marks in "show the steps" are the steps, not the number.
methodFrames.ask: Last: recursion against iteration. One advantage each.

methodFrames.check: Recursion is clearer for recursive definitions; iteration is faster and safer on memory.
methodFrames.teach: Recursion is shorter and closer to the definition for problems that are naturally recursive, factorials, Fibonacci, tree walks. Iteration uses no call stack, so it is faster and cannot overflow. Any recursive method can be written as a loop, and the exam sometimes asks for both.

exam.answer:
Q6 b · what does compute(13) return? show the steps · 3 MARKS

The answer: 3. And the question says show the steps, so the table is the answer, not the number.

Dry run · compute(13), step by step
while (x > 0): count the odd steps, halve each time
xx % 2odd, so count++?x = x / 2count
131yes61
60no31
31yes12
11yes03
0x > 0 is false, so the loop ends3

What the method actually is. Repeatedly halving with x / 2 and testing x % 2 walks the number's binary digits, from the right. So compute counts the 1 bits. 13 in binary is 1101, which has three 1s, so the answer is 3, and you can check it in one second without tracing anything.

Say that in your answer after showing the table. Naming what the code is ("it counts the set bits") is what separates a trace from understanding, and it costs one line.

Code · the paper's own method, run on 13 and on friends · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ComputeBits {    // exactly as the paper prints it    public static int compute(int x) {        int count = 0;        while (x > 0) {            if (x % 2 == 1) count++;            x = x / 2;        }        return count;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("compute(13) = " + compute(13));        System.out.println("13 in binary is " + Integer.toBinaryString(13));        for (int v : new int[]{1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 255}) {            System.out.println("compute(" + v + ") = " + compute(v)                + "   binary " + Integer.toBinaryString(v));        }    }}
Outputcompute(13) = 3
13 in binary is 1101
compute(1) = 1   binary 1
compute(2) = 1   binary 10
compute(3) = 2   binary 11
compute(7) = 3   binary 111
compute(8) = 1   binary 1000
compute(255) = 8   binary 11111111

Every row is its own proof: the answer always equals the number of 1s printed beside it. compute(255) = 8 and 255 is eight 1s; compute(8) = 1 and 8 is 1000. The claim is not "this looks like a bit count", it is a bit count.
